sources.title: Newer Pharmacologic Treatments in Adults With Type 2 Diabetes: A Clinical Guideline From the American College of Physicians.
authors: Clinical Guidelines Committee of the American College of Physicians
sources.excerpt: RECOMMENDATION 1: ACP recommends adding a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT-2) inhibitor or glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) agonist to metformin and lifestyle modifications in adults with type 2 diabetes and inadequate glycemic control (strong recommendation; high-certainty evidence). • Use an SGLT-2 inhibitor to reduce the risk for all-cause mortality, major adverse cardiovascular events, progression of chronic kidney disease, and hospitalization due to congestive heart failure. • Use a GLP-1 agonist to reduce the risk for all-cause mortality, major adverse cardiovascular events, and stroke. RECOMMENDATION 2: ACP recommends against adding a dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitor to metformin and lifestyle modifications in adults with type 2 diabetes and inadequate glycemic control to reduce morbidity and all-cause mortality (strong recommendation; high-certainty evidence).

sources.title: Cardiovascular, kidney related, and weight loss effects of therapeutics for type 2 diabetes: a living clinical practice guideline.
sources.excerpt: RECOMMENDATIONS: The panel issued risk-stratified recommendations regarding four prioritised medications for adults with type 2 diabetes (SGLT-2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, finerenone and tirzepatide):• Lower risk (three or fewer cardiovascular risk factors without established cardiovascular disease (CVD) or chronic kidney disease (CKD)): weak recommendation against SGLT-2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists.• Moderate risk (more than three cardiovascular risk factors without established CVD or CKD; or established CVD and/or CKD at lower risk of complications): weak recommendation in favour of SGLT-2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists; and a weak recommendation against finerenone in adults with CKD.• Higher risk (established CVD and/or CKD at higher risk of complications, or established heart failure): strong recommendation in favour of SGLT-2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists; and a weak recommendation in favour of finerenone in adults with CKD.• Across risk strata: weak recommendation in favour of tirzepatide in adults with obesity. … Recommendations were informed by a linked living systematic review and network meta-analysis evaluating relative benefits and harms updated to 31 July 2024; and by linked systematic reviews addressing risk prediction models and values and preferences of adults with type 2 diabetes.

sources.title: Diabetes Management in Chronic Kidney Disease: Synopsis of the KDIGO 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline Update.
sources.excerpt: DESCRIPTION: The KDIGO 2022 Clinical Practice Guideline for Diabetes Management in Chronic Kidney Disease is an update of the 2020 guideline from Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO). … A focus on preserving kidney function and maintaining well-being is recommended using a layered approach to care, starting with a foundation of lifestyle interventions, self-management, and first-line pharmacotherapy (such as sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors) demonstrated to improve clinical outcomes. To this are added additional drugs with heart and kidney protection, such as glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists and nonsteroidal mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and interventions to control risk factors for CKD progression and cardiovascular events, such as blood pressure, glycemia, and lipids.

sources.title: American Association of Clinical Endocrinology Consensus Statement: Algorithm for Management of Adults With Type 2 Diabetes - 2026 Update.
sources.publisher: Endocrine practice : official journal of the American College of Endocrinology and the American Association of Clinical Endocrinologists
sources.excerpt: RESULTS: This algorithm for management of adults with type 2 diabetes (T2D) includes 11 sections: (1) Principles for the Management of Adults With T2D; (2) Prediabetes Algorithm (3) Diabetes Classification Algorithm (new); (4) Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease Risk Reduction Algorithm: Dyslipidemia; (5) Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease Risk Reduction Algorithm: Hypertension; (6) Comorbidities- and Complications-Centric Glycemic Control Algorithm; (7) Glucose-Centric Glycemic Control Algorithm; (8) Initiating and Titrating Insulin Algorithm; (9) Profiles of Pharmacotherapy for T2D; (10) Profiles of Pharmacotherapy for Obesity; and (11) Vaccine Recommendations for Adults With T2D. CONCLUSIONS: This 2026 update emphasizes lifestyle modification and treatment of overweight/obesity as key pillars in the management of prediabetes and T2D. It also provides guidance on the management of atherosclerotic risk factors of dyslipidemia and hypertension.

sources.title: Clinical Practice Guideline: Shared Decision Making, Diagnostic Evaluation, and Pharmacotherapy in Type 2 Diabetes.
sources.issuing_body: German National Disease Management Guideline (NVL) programme
authors: the National Disease Management Guideline Group
sources.excerpt: RESULTS: The new chapter on shared decision making includes a description of a structured approach that can be used when individual treatment goals have not been achieved. … Cardiovascular and renal risks are to be considered in the choice of drug. Studies have shown that, in persons with cardiovascular disease, treatment with GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1, glucagon-like peptide-1) or SGLT2 inhibitors (SGLT2, sodium-glucose co-transporter-2) was less likely than the comparison intervention to lead to certain patient-relevant endpoints, including all-cause mortality (OR = 0.88 and 0.84, respectively), hospitalization for heart failure (SGLT2 inhibitors: OR = 0.65), and worsening of renal function (OR = 0.61 and 0.59, respectively). CONCLUSION: Current evidence continues to support the recommendations on pharmacotherapy of the 2021 guideline. The Guideline Group did not find evidence of adequate certainty to inform recommendations about the screening of persons at risk, HbA1c target values, or screening for sequelae and comorbidities.

sources.title: Exercise/Physical Activity in Individuals with Type 2 Diabetes: A Consensus Statement from the American College of Sports Medicine.
sources.publisher: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
sources.excerpt: This consensus statement is an update of the 2010 American College of Sports Medicine position stand on exercise and type 2 diabetes. … Various types of physical activity enhance health and glycemic management in people with type 2 diabetes, including flexibility and balance exercise, and the importance of each recommended type or mode are discussed. In general, the 2018 Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans apply to all individuals with type 2 diabetes, with a few exceptions and modifications. People with type 2 diabetes should engage in physical activity regularly and be encouraged to reduce sedentary time and break up sitting time with frequent activity breaks.

sources.title: Newer Pharmacologic Treatments in Adults With Type 2 Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-analysis for the American College of Physicians.
sources.excerpt: Compared with usual care, SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP1 agonists reduce all-cause mortality (high CoE) and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) (moderate to high CoE), SGLT2 inhibitors reduce progression of chronic kidney disease (CKD) and heart failure hospitalizations and GLP1 agonists reduce stroke (high CoE), and SGLT2 inhibitors reduce serious adverse events and severe hypoglycemia (high CoE). … Compared with usual care, insulin, tirzepatide, and DPP4 inhibitors do not reduce all-cause mortality (low to high CoE). … Compared with DPP4 inhibitors, GLP1 agonists reduce all-cause mortality (moderate CoE). Compared with DPP4 inhibitors and sulfonylurea (SU), SGLT2 inhibitors reduce MACE (moderate to high CoE). … Serious adverse events and severe hypoglycemia are less frequent with SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP1 agonists than with insulin or SU.

sources.title: Hemoglobin A1c Targets for Glycemic Control With Pharmacologic Therapy for Nonpregnant Adults With Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Guidance Statement Update From the American College of Physicians.
authors: Clinical Guidelines Committee of the American College of Physicians
sources.tier_rationale: Rule: title identifies a guidance document ('Guidance Statement'); PubMed indexes it as 'Journal Article, Research Support, Non-U.S. Gov't, Review'
sources.excerpt: GUIDANCE STATEMENT 1: Clinicians should personalize goals for glycemic control in patients with type 2 diabetes on the basis of a discussion of benefits and harms of pharmacotherapy, patients' preferences, patients' general health and life expectancy, treatment burden, and costs of care. GUIDANCE STATEMENT 2: Clinicians should aim to achieve an HbA1c level between 7% and 8% in most patients with type 2 diabetes. GUIDANCE STATEMENT 3: Clinicians should consider deintensifying pharmacologic therapy in patients with type 2 diabetes who achieve HbA1c levels less than 6.5%. GUIDANCE STATEMENT 4: Clinicians should treat patients with type 2 diabetes to minimize symptoms related to hyperglycemia and avoid targeting an HbA1c level in patients with a life expectancy less than 10 years due to advanced age (80 years or older), residence in a nursing home, or chronic conditions (such as dementia, cancer, end-stage kidney disease, or severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or congestive heart failure) because the harms outweigh the benefits in this population.

sources.title: Diabetes Type 2
sources.issuing_body: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases
sources.tier_rationale: Rule: MedlinePlus health topic (NLM-curated consumer health summary)
sources.excerpt:
What is type 2 diabetes?

Type 2 diabetes is a disease in which your blood glucose, or blood sugar, levels are too high. Glucose is your main source of energy. It comes from the foods you eat. A hormone called insulin helps the glucose get into your cells to give them energy. If you have diabetes, your body doesn't make enough insulin or doesn't use insulin well. The glucose then stays in your blood and not enough goes into your cells.

Over time, having too much glucose in your blood can cause health problems. But you can take steps to manage your diabetes and try to prevent these health problems.

What causes type 2 diabetes?

Type 2 diabetes may be caused by a combination of factors:

- Being overweight or having obesity
- Not being physically active
- Genetics and family history

Type 2 diabetes usually starts with insulin resistance. This is a condition in which your cells don't respond normally to insulin. As a result, your body needs more insulin to help the glucose enter your cells. At first, your body makes more insulin to try to get cells to respond. But over time, your body can't make enough insulin, and your blood glucose levels rise.

Who is at risk for type 2 diabetes?

You are at higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes if you:

- Are over age 45. Children, teenagers, and younger adults can get type 2 diabetes, but it is more common in middle-aged and older people.
- Have prediabetes, which means that your blood glucose is high for you but not high enough to be called diabetes
- Had diabetes in pregnancy or gave birth to a baby weighing 9 pounds or more.
- Have a family history of diabetes
- Are overweight or have obesity
- Are Black or African American, Hispanic/Latino, American Indian, Asian American, or Pacific Islander
- Are not physically active
- Have other conditions such as high blood pressure, heart disease, stroke, polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), or depression
- Have low HDL (good) cholesterol and high triglycerides
- Have acanthosis nigricans - dark, thick, and velvety skin around your neck or armpitsWhat are the symptoms of type 2 diabetes?

Many people with type 2 diabetes have no symptoms at all. If you do have them, the symptoms develop slowly over several years. They might be so mild that you do not notice them. The symptoms can include:

- Increased thirst and urination
- Increased hunger
- Feeling tired
- Blurred vision
- Numbness or tingling in the feet or hands
- Sores that do not heal
- Unexplained weight lossHow is type 2 diabetes diagnosed?

Your provider will use blood tests to diagnose type 2 diabetes. The blood tests include:

- A1C test, which measures your average blood glucose level over the past 3 months.
- Fasting plasma glucose (FPG) test, which measures your current blood glucose level. You need to fast (not eat or drink anything except water) for at least 8 hours before the test.
- Random plasma glucose (RPG) test, which measures your current blood glucose level. This test is used when you have diabetes symptoms and the provider does not want to wait for you to fast before having the test.What are the treatments for type 2 diabetes?

Treatment for type 2 diabetes involves managing your blood glucose levels. Many people are able to do this by living a healthy lifestyle. Some people may also need to take medicine:

- A healthy lifestyle includes following a healthy eating plan and getting regular physical activity. You need to learn how to balance what you eat and drink with physical activity and diabetes medicine, if you take any.
- Medicines for diabetes include oral medicines, insulin, and other injectable medicines. Over time, some people will need to take more than one type of medicine to control their diabetes.
- You will need to check your blood glucose regularly. Your provider will tell you how often you need to do it.
- It's also important to keep your blood pressure and cholesterol levels close to the targets your provider sets for you. Make sure to get your screening tests regularly.Can type 2 diabetes be prevented?

You can take steps to help prevent or delay type 2 diabetes by losing weight if you are overweight, eating fewer calories, and being more physically active. If you have a condition which raises your risk for type 2 diabetes, managing that condition may lower your risk of getting type 2 diabetes.

evidence.quote: Clinicians should consider deintensifying pharmacologic therapy in patients with type 2 diabetes who achieve HbA1c levels less than 6.5%.
evidence.statement: Drug therapy should be reduced when HbA1c falls below 6.5%.

evidence.quote: avoid targeting an HbA1c level in patients with a life expectancy less than 10 years due to advanced age (80 years or older), residence in a nursing home, or chronic conditions
evidence.statement: For people with limited life expectancy, treat symptoms rather than an HbA1c target.

treatment_options.suggestion_reason: Supports overtreatment reduction in older and frail populations.

treatment_options.name: Structured shared decision making
treatment_options.population: Adults whose individual treatment goals have not been achieved
treatment_options.summary: The German NDMG adds a structured shared-decision-making approach for use when individual treatment goals are not met.

evidence.quote: The new chapter on shared decision making includes a description of a structured approach that can be used when individual treatment goals have not been achieved.
evidence.statement: The guideline adds a structured shared-decision-making process.

treatment_options.suggestion_reason: Process recommendation from one non-US guideline; better covered in a care-model briefing.

treatment_options.name: Blood pressure and lipid management
treatment_options.summary: KDIGO, AACE and MedlinePlus all include control of blood pressure and lipids alongside glycemia to reduce cardiovascular and kidney events.

evidence.quote: interventions to control risk factors for CKD progression and cardiovascular events, such as blood pressure, glycemia, and lipids
evidence.statement: Blood pressure, glucose and lipid control are part of comprehensive care.

evidence.quote: It also provides guidance on the management of atherosclerotic risk factors of dyslipidemia and hypertension.
evidence.statement: The algorithm covers lipid and blood pressure management as part of diabetes care.

evidence.quote: It's also important to keep your blood pressure and cholesterol levels close to the targets your provider sets for you.
evidence.statement: Blood pressure and cholesterol should be kept near individual targets.

treatment_options.suggestion_reason: Important but usually covered by a separate cardiometabolic risk briefing.

treatment_options.name: Blood glucose self-monitoring
treatment_options.summary: MedlinePlus advises regular blood glucose checks at a frequency set by the provider; no guideline in this set grades it.

evidence.quote: You will need to check your blood glucose regularly. Your provider will tell you how often you need to do it.
evidence.statement: People with type 2 diabetes check their blood glucose regularly as advised.

treatment_options.suggestion_reason: Supported only by a consumer health summary in this set; no graded guideline evidence.

conflicts.topic: Should SGLT-2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists be added for adults at lower cardiovascular and kidney risk?

positions.statement: ACP strongly recommends adding an SGLT-2 inhibitor or GLP-1 agonist to metformin for all adults with inadequate glycemic control, without stratifying by cardiovascular or kidney risk.
positions.quote: ACP recommends adding a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT-2) inhibitor or glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) agonist to metformin and lifestyle modifications in adults with type 2 diabetes and inadequate glycemic control (strong recommendation; high-certainty evidence).

positions.statement: The BMJ living guideline gives a weak recommendation against SGLT-2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists for adults with three or fewer cardiovascular risk factors and no established CVD or CKD.
positions.quote: Lower risk (three or fewer cardiovascular risk factors without established cardiovascular disease (CVD) or chronic kidney disease (CKD)): weak recommendation against SGLT-2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists.

conflicts.ai_assessment: Both are recent tier-1 guidelines, but they frame the decision differently: ACP (US, April 2024) keys the recommendation to inadequate glycemic control on metformin, whereas the BMJ international panel (August 2025) stratifies by absolute cardiovascular and kidney risk and weighs burden and cost from an individual patient perspective. For lower-risk adults the two directly disagree. The BMJ evidence base is newer (living review to July 2024); ACP is the US college of internists.

suggested_resolution.rationale: Rule (same tier, newer wins): position 2: tier 1 clinical guideline (2025-08-14) is more recent than position 1: tier 1 clinical guideline (2024-04-19). This is a recency rule, not a judgement of the evidence.

conflicts.topic: What HbA1c target should guide drug therapy for most adults with type 2 diabetes?

positions.statement: ACP sets a target HbA1c between 7% and 8% for most patients and advises deintensifying below 6.5%.
positions.quote: Clinicians should aim to achieve an HbA1c level between 7% and 8% in most patients with type 2 diabetes.

positions.statement: The German national guideline group found no evidence of adequate certainty to make any recommendation on HbA1c target values.
positions.quote: The Guideline Group did not find evidence of adequate certainty to inform recommendations about the screening of persons at risk, HbA1c target values, or screening for sequelae and comorbidities.

conflicts.ai_assessment: ACP's 2018 guidance statement (US) derives a numeric range from an appraisal of other national guidelines, while the 2023 German national guideline declines to recommend a target because evidence certainty is inadequate. The German source is newer; PubMed indexes the ACP statement as a review, so its guideline tier comes from its title. Both agree that goals should be individualised.

suggested_resolution.rationale: Rule (same tier, newer wins): position 2: tier 1 clinical guideline (2023-11-24) is more recent than position 1: tier 1 clinical guideline (2018-03-06). This is a recency rule, not a judgement of the evidence.

conflicts.topic: Is an SGLT-2 inhibitor first-line, or an add-on to metformin, when chronic kidney disease is present?

positions.statement: ACP positions SGLT-2 inhibitors and GLP-1 agonists as additions to metformin and lifestyle modification for adults with inadequate glycemic control, without a separate CKD pathway.
positions.quote: ACP recommends adding a sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT-2) inhibitor or glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) agonist to metformin and lifestyle modifications in adults with type 2 diabetes and inadequate glycemic control (strong recommendation; high-certainty evidence).

positions.statement: For people with diabetes and CKD, KDIGO names SGLT-2 inhibitors as first-line pharmacotherapy on a foundation of lifestyle and self-management.
positions.quote: A focus on preserving kidney function and maintaining well-being is recommended using a layered approach to care, starting with a foundation of lifestyle interventions, self-management, and first-line pharmacotherapy (such as sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 inhibitors) demonstrated to improve clinical outcomes.

conflicts.ai_assessment: The two guidelines address different populations. ACP (2024) addresses adults with type 2 diabetes and inadequate glycemic control in general and places SGLT-2 inhibitors after metformin. KDIGO (2022) addresses people with diabetes and chronic kidney disease and names SGLT-2 inhibitors as first-line pharmacotherapy because of their kidney and cardiovascular outcomes. Neither source states a position on the other population.

suggested_resolution.rationale: Population difference: the positions apply to different patient groups, so they are kept with the population stated.
